[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/de/mod.rs.html#1253-1255)#### fn [is_human_readable](https://docs.rs#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/de/mod.rs.html#1253-1255)

#### fn [is_human_readable](https://docs.rs#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

Determine whether `Deserialize` implementations should expect to
deserialize their human-readable form.

Some types have a human-readable form that may be somewhat expensive to construct, as well as a binary form that is compact and efficient. Generally text-based formats like JSON and YAML will prefer to use the human-readable one and binary formats like Postcard will prefer the compact one.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::de::{self, Deserialize, Deserializer};
impl<'de> Deserialize<'de> for Timestamp {
    fn deserialize<D>(deserializer: D) -> Result<Self, D::Error>
    where
        D: Deserializer<'de>,
    {
        if deserializer.is_human_readable() {
            // Deserialize from a human-readable string like "2015-05-15T17:01:00Z".
            let s = String::deserialize(deserializer)?;
            Timestamp::from_str(&s).map_err(de::Error::custom)
        } else {
            // Deserialize from a compact binary representation, seconds since
            // the Unix epoch.
            let n = u64::deserialize(deserializer)?;
            Ok(Timestamp::EPOCH + Duration::seconds(n))
        }
    }
}
```
The default implementation of this method returns `true`. Data formats
may override this to `false` to request a compact form for types that
support one. Note that modifying this method to change a format from
human-readable to compact or vice versa should be regarded as a breaking
change, as a value serialized in human-readable mode is not required to
deserialize from the same data in compact mode.

# Serialize in serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0/trait.Serialize.html

```
pub trait Serialize {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[serialize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize)<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<S::[Ok](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Ok), S::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where S: [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html);
}## Expand description

A **data structure** that can be serialized into any data format supported
by Serde.

Serde provides `Serialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
standard library types. The complete list is [here](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html). All of
these can be serialized using Serde out of the box.

Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called [ serde_derive](https://crates.io/crates/serde_derive) to
automatically generate

`Serialize` implementations for structs and enums in
your program. See the [derive section of the manual](https://serde.rs/derive.html)for how to use this.

In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Serialize` manually for some
type in your program. See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the
manual for more about this.

Third-party crates may provide `Serialize` implementations for types that
they expose. For example the [ linked-hash-map](https://crates.io/crates/linked-hash-map) crate provides a

[type that is serializable by Serde because the crate provides an implementation of](https://docs.rs/linked-hash-map/*/linked_hash_map/struct.LinkedHashMap.html)

`LinkedHashMap<K, V>``Serialize` for it.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Serialize this value into the given Serde serializer.

See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the manual for more
information about how to implement this method.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeStruct, Serializer};
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
// This is what #[derive(Serialize)] would generate.
impl Serialize for Person {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut s = serializer.serialize_struct("Person", 3)?;
        s.serialize_field("name", &self.name)?;
        s.serialize_field("age", &self.age)?;
        s.serialize_field("phones", &self.phones)?;
        s.end()
    }
}
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/impls.rs.html#492-504)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-Rc%3CT%3E)Available on **crate feature **`rc` and (crate features `std` or `alloc`) only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/impls.rs.html#492-504)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-Rc%3CT%3E)

**crate feature**only.

`rc` and (crate features `std` or `alloc`)Serializing a data structure containing `Rc` will serialize a copy of
the contents of the `Rc` each time the `Rc` is referenced within the
data structure. Serialization will not attempt to deduplicate these
repeated data.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/impls.rs.html#506-518)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-Arc%3CT%3E)Available on **crate feature **`rc` and (crate features `std` or `alloc`) only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/impls.rs.html#506-518)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Serialize-for-Arc%3CT%3E)

**crate feature**only.

`rc` and (crate features `std` or `alloc`)Serializing a data structure containing `Arc` will serialize a copy of
the contents of the `Arc` each time the `Arc` is referenced within the
data structure. Serialization will not attempt to deduplicate these
repeated data.

}## Expand description

A **data format** that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

The role of this trait is to define the serialization half of the [Serde
data model](https://serde.rs/data-model.html), which is a way to categorize every Rust data structure into one
of 29 possible types. Each method of the `Serializer` trait corresponds to
one of the types of the data model.

Implementations of `Serialize` map themselves into this data model by
invoking exactly one of the `Serializer` methods.

The types that make up the Serde data model are:

- **14 primitive types**- bool
- i8, i16, i32, i64, i128
- u8, u16, u32, u64, u128
- f32, f64
- char

- **string**- UTF-8 bytes with a length and no null terminator.
- When serializing, all strings are handled equally. When deserializing, there are three flavors of strings: transient, owned, and borrowed.

- **byte array**- [u8]- Similar to strings, during deserialization byte arrays can be transient, owned, or borrowed.

- **option**- Either none or some value.

- **unit**- The type of `()`in Rust. It represents an anonymous value containing no data.

- The type of
- **unit_struct**- For example `struct Unit`or`PhantomData<T>`. It represents a named value containing no data.

- For example
- **unit_variant**- For example the `E::A`and`E::B`in`enum E { A, B }`.

- For example the
- **newtype_struct**- For example `struct Millimeters(u8)`.

- For example
- **newtype_variant**- For example the `E::N`in`enum E { N(u8) }`.

- For example the
- **seq**- A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example
`Vec<T>`or`HashSet<T>`. When serializing, the length may or may not be known before iterating through all the data. When deserializing, the length is determined by looking at the serialized data.

- A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example
- **tuple**- A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example `(u8,)`or`(String, u64, Vec<T>)`or`[u64; 10]`.

- A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example
- **tuple_struct**- A named tuple, for example `struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8)`.

- A named tuple, for example
- **tuple_variant**- For example the `E::T`in`enum E { T(u8, u8) }`.

- For example the
- **map**- A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example `BTreeMap<K, V>`.

- A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example
- **struct**- A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example `struct S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 }`.

- A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example
- **struct_variant**- For example the `E::S`in`enum E { S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 } }`.

- For example the

Many Serde serializers produce text or binary data as output, for example
JSON or Postcard. This is not a requirement of the `Serializer` trait, and
there are serializers that do not produce text or binary output. One example
is the `serde_json::value::Serializer` (distinct from the main `serde_json`
serializer) that produces a `serde_json::Value` data structure in memory as
output.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-implementation)Example implementation

The [example data format](https://serde.rs/data-format.html) presented on the website contains example code for
a basic JSON `Serializer`.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

The output type produced by this `Serializer` during successful
serialization. Most serializers that produce text or binary output
should set `Ok = ()` and serialize into an [ io::Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Write.html) or buffer
contained within the

`Serializer` instance. Serializers that build
in-memory data structures may be simplified by using `Ok` to propagate
the data structure around.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Serialize an `i8` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i8` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize an `i16` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i16` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize an `i32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i32` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize a `u8` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u8` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize a `u16` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u16` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize a `u32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u32` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize an `f32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `f32` and `f64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `f64` and
forward to `serialize_f64`.

Serialize a character.

If the format does not support characters, it is reasonable to serialize
it as a single element `str` or a `u32`.

Serialize a chunk of raw byte data.

Enables serializers to serialize byte slices more compactly or more
efficiently than other types of slices. If no efficient implementation
is available, a reasonable implementation would be to forward to
`serialize_seq`. If forwarded, the implementation looks usually just
like this:

Serialize a unit struct like `struct Unit` or `PhantomData<T>`.

A reasonable implementation would be to forward to `serialize_unit`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
struct Nothing;
impl Serialize for Nothing {

    where
        S: Serializer,

        serializer.serialize_unit_struct("Nothing")
    }

Serialize a unit variant like `E::A` in `enum E { A, B }`.

The `name` is the name of the enum, the `variant_index` is the index of
this variant within the enum, and the `variant` is the name of the
variant.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
enum E {
    A,
    B,
}
impl Serialize for E {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        match *self {
            E::A => serializer.serialize_unit_variant("E", 0, "A"),
            E::B => serializer.serialize_unit_variant("E", 1, "B"),
        }
    }
}

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#916-922)

Serialize a newtype struct like `struct Millimeters(u8)`.

Serializers are encouraged to treat newtype structs as insignificant
wrappers around the data they contain. A reasonable implementation would
be to forward to `value.serialize(self)`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
struct Millimeters(u8);
impl Serialize for Millimeters {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.serialize_newtype_struct("Millimeters", &self.0)
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#950-958)

Serialize a newtype variant like `E::N` in `enum E { N(u8) }`.

The `name` is the name of the enum, the `variant_index` is the index of

variant. The `value` is the data contained within this newtype variant.

#### fn [serialize_seq](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_seq)(
    self,
    len: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html)>,

Begin to serialize a variably sized sequence. This call must be
followed by zero or more calls to `serialize_element`, then a call to
`end`.

The argument is the number of elements in the sequence, which may or may not be computable before the sequence is iterated. Some serializers only support sequences whose length is known up front.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeSeq, Serializer};
impl<T> Serialize for Vec<T>
where
    T: Serialize,
{
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut seq = serializer.serialize_seq(Some(self.len()))?;
        for element in self {
            seq.serialize_element(element)?;
        }
        seq.end()
    }
}
```

Begin to serialize a statically sized sequence whose length will be
known at deserialization time without looking at the serialized data.
This call must be followed by zero or more calls to `serialize_element`,
then a call to `end`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeTuple, Serializer};
impl<A, B, C> Serialize for (A, B, C)
where
    A: Serialize,
    B: Serialize,
    C: Serialize,
{
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut tup = serializer.serialize_tuple(3)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.0)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.1)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.2)?;
        tup.end()
    }
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeTuple, Serializer};
const VRAM_SIZE: usize = 386;
struct Vram([u16; VRAM_SIZE]);
impl Serialize for Vram {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut seq = serializer.serialize_tuple(VRAM_SIZE)?;
        for element in &self.0[..] {
            seq.serialize_element(element)?;
        }
        seq.end()
    }
}

                let mut tv = serializer.serialize_tuple_variant("E", 1, "U", 3)?;

#### fn [serialize_map](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_map)(
    self,
    len: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html)>,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[SerializeMap](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.SerializeMap), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

Begin to serialize a map. This call must be followed by zero or more
calls to `serialize_key` and `serialize_value`, then a call to `end`.

The argument is the number of elements in the map, which may or may not be computable before the map is iterated. Some serializers only support maps whose length is known up front.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeMap, Serializer};
impl<K, V> Serialize for HashMap<K, V>
where
    K: Serialize,
    V: Serialize,
{
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut map = serializer.serialize_map(Some(self.len()))?;
        for (k, v) in self {
            map.serialize_entry(k, v)?;
        }
        map.end()
    }
}
```

Collect an iterator as a sequence.

The default implementation serializes each item yielded by the iterator
using [ serialize_seq](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_seq). Implementors should not need to override this
method.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
struct SecretlyOneHigher {
    data: Vec<i32>,
}
impl Serialize for SecretlyOneHigher {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.collect_seq(self.data.iter().map(|x| x + 1))
    }
}

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#1459-1461)

#### fn [is_human_readable](https://docs.rs#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

Determine whether `Serialize` implementations should serialize in
human-readable form.

Some types have a human-readable form that may be somewhat expensive to construct, as well as a binary form that is compact and efficient. Generally text-based formats like JSON and YAML will prefer to use the human-readable one and binary formats like Postcard will prefer the compact one.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
impl Serialize for Timestamp {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        if serializer.is_human_readable() {
            // Serialize to a human-readable string "2015-05-15T17:01:00Z".
            self.to_string().serialize(serializer)
        } else {
            // Serialize to a compact binary representation.
            self.seconds_since_epoch().serialize(serializer)
        }
    }
}
```
The default implementation of this method returns `true`. Data formats
may override this to `false` to request a compact form for types that
support one. Note that modifying this method to change a format from
human-readable to compact or vice versa should be regarded as a breaking
change, as a value serialized in human-readable mode is not required to
deserialize from the same data in compact mode.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

## Implementations on Foreign Types[§](https://docs.rs#foreign-impls)

    StartRequest,
    EndRequest,
}
impl Display for MessageType {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        self.serialize(f)
    }
}
```

# atree - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/atree/0.5.4/i686-pc-windows-msvc/atree/

## Expand description

An arena based tree structure, backed by a custom allocator (ultimately
built on `Vec`) that makes node removal a possibility. On top of the basic
node insertion and removal operations, there are also many kinds of
immutable and mutable iterators provided for various kinds of tree traversal
operations.

Most of the code in the crate is `unsafe` free, except for the mutable
iterators, where the `unsafe` code is lifted from the core Rust
implementation of `IterMut`.

[§](https://docs.rs#general-guide-to-the-api)General Guide to the API

The crate consists of three main `struct`s: [ Arena<T>](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html),

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)

`Token`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Node.html)

`Node<T>``Arena<T>` provides the arena in which all data is stored.
The data can then be accessed by indexing `Arena<T>` with `Token`. `Node<T>`
is a container that encapsulates the data on the tree.As a general rule of thumb, methods that affect the memory layout such as
splitting and merging arenas, or methods to create and destroy nodes regardless
of existing tree structures like creating a free node, are defined on
`Arena<T>`. Methods that alter pre-existing tree structures such as adding
nodes with respect to existing ones ([ append](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html#method.append) or

[for instance) or splitting and attaching existing trees are defined on](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html#method.insert_after)

`insert_after``Tokens`.When it comes to iterating, iterators can be created from methods on both
`Token` and `Node<T>`. There are two versions of iterators, iterators over
tokens or references to the nodes. Both can be created by methods on `Token`
and `Node<T>`. However, due to the rules of borrow checking, mutable
iterators over the node references are only defined on `Token`.

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

- `serde`: support for serde 1.x. Optional feature/dependency.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage-examples)Usage Examples

We can start by initializing an empty arena and add stuff to it at a later time:

```
use atree::Arena;
let mut arena = Arena::default();
assert!(arena.is_empty());
// create a tree in the arena
let data = "Indo-European";
let token = arena.new_node(data);
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 1)
```
There is a shortcut to the above operation:

```
use atree::Arena;
let data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, token) = Arena::with_data(data);
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 1)
```
To add more data to the tree, call the [ append](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html#method.append) method on the tokens (we
can’t do this directly to the nodes because of the limitations of borrow
checking).

```
use atree::Arena;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 2);
```
To access/modify existing nodes in the tree, we can use indexing or
[ get](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.get)/

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.get_mut)

`get_mut````
use atree::Arena;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
// add some more stuff to the tree
let branch1 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
let branch2 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let branch3 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Slavic");
let lang1 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "English");
let lang2 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "Swedish");
let lang3 = branch3.append(&mut arena, "Polish");
// Access data by indexing the arena by a token. This operation panics if the
// token is invalid.
assert_eq!(arena[branch3].data, "Slavic");
// Access data by calling "get" on the arena with a token.
assert_eq!(arena.get(lang1).unwrap().data, "English");
// We can also do so mutably (with "get" or through indexing). As you can
// see, calling the "get" functions is more verbose but you get to avoid
// surprise panic attacks (if you don't unwrap like I do here).
arena.get_mut(lang1).unwrap().data = "Icelandic";
assert_eq!(arena[lang1].data, "Icelandic");
// On the flip side, we can access the corresponding token if we already
// have the node
let branch3_node = &arena[branch3];
assert_eq!(branch3, branch3_node.token());
```
We can iterate over the elements by calling iterators on both the tokens
or the nodes. Check the documentation of [ Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html) or

[for a list of iterators. There is a version of each of the iterators that iterates over tokens instead of node references. See the docs for details.](https://docs.rs/struct.Node.html)

`Node<T>````
use atree::Arena;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
// add some more stuff to the tree
let branch1 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
let branch2 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let branch3 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Slavic");
let lang1 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "English");
let lang2 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "Swedish");
let lang3 = branch3.append(&mut arena, "Polish");
// Getting an iterator from a token and iterate
let children: Vec<_> = root_token.children(&arena).map(|x| x.data).collect();
assert_eq!(&["Romance", "Germanic", "Slavic"], &children[..]);
// Getting an iterator from a node reference (that is if you already have it
// around. To go out of your way to get the node reference before getting
// the iterator seems kind of dumb).
let polish = &arena[lang3];
let ancestors: Vec<_> = polish.ancestors(&arena).map(|x| x.data).collect();
assert_eq!(&["Slavic", "Indo-European"], &ancestors[..]);
// We can also iterate mutably. Unfortunately we can only get mutable
// iterators from the tokens but not from the node references because of
// borrow checking.
for lang in branch2.children_mut(&mut arena) {
    lang.data = "Not romantic enough";
}
assert_eq!(arena[lang1].data, "Not romantic enough");
assert_eq!(arena[lang2].data, "Not romantic enough");
```
To remove a single node from the arena, use the [ remove](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.remove) method. This will
detach all the children of the node from the tree (but not remove them from
memory).

```
use atree::Arena;
use atree::iter::TraversalOrder;
// root node that we will attach subtrees to
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
// the Germanic branch
let germanic = root.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let west = germanic.append(&mut arena, "West");
let scots = west.append(&mut arena, "Scots");
let english = west.append(&mut arena, "English");
// detach the west branch from the main tree
let west_children = arena.remove(west);
// the west branch is gone from the original tree
let mut iter = root.subtree(&arena, TraversalOrder::Pre)
    .map(|x| x.data);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Indo-European"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Germanic"));
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
// its children are still areound
let mut iter = west_children.iter().map(|&t| arena[t].data);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Scots"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("English"));
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
```
To uproot a tree from the arena, call the [ uproot](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.uproot) method on the arena.
Note that will also remove all descendants of the node. After removal, the
“freed” memory will be reused if and when new data is inserted.

```
use atree::Arena;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
// add some more stuff to the tree
let branch1 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
let branch2 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let branch3 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Slavic");
let lang1 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "English");
let lang2 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "Swedish");
let lang3 = branch3.append(&mut arena, "Polish");
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 7);
arena.uproot(branch2);  // boring languages anyway
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 4);
```

# atree - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/atree/latest/target-redirect/i686-pc-windows-msvc/atree/index.html

## Expand description

An arena based tree structure, backed by a custom allocator (ultimately
built on `Vec`) that makes node removal a possibility. On top of the basic
node insertion and removal operations, there are also many kinds of
immutable and mutable iterators provided for various kinds of tree traversal
operations.

Most of the code in the crate is `unsafe` free, except for the mutable
iterators, where the `unsafe` code is lifted from the core Rust
implementation of `IterMut`.

[§](https://docs.rs#general-guide-to-the-api)General Guide to the API

The crate consists of three main `struct`s: [ Arena<T>](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html),

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)

`Token`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Node.html)

`Node<T>``Arena<T>` provides the arena in which all data is stored.
The data can then be accessed by indexing `Arena<T>` with `Token`. `Node<T>`
is a container that encapsulates the data on the tree.As a general rule of thumb, methods that affect the memory layout such as
splitting and merging arenas, or methods to create and destroy nodes regardless
of existing tree structures like creating a free node, are defined on
`Arena<T>`. Methods that alter pre-existing tree structures such as adding
nodes with respect to existing ones ([ append](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html#method.append) or

[for instance) or splitting and attaching existing trees are defined on](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html#method.insert_after)

`insert_after``Tokens`.When it comes to iterating, iterators can be created from methods on both
`Token` and `Node<T>`. There are two versions of iterators, iterators over
tokens or references to the nodes. Both can be created by methods on `Token`
and `Node<T>`. However, due to the rules of borrow checking, mutable
iterators over the node references are only defined on `Token`.

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

- `serde`: support for serde 1.x. Optional feature/dependency.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage-examples)Usage Examples

We can start by initializing an empty arena and add stuff to it at a later time:

```
use atree::Arena;
let mut arena = Arena::default();
assert!(arena.is_empty());
// create a tree in the arena
let data = "Indo-European";
let token = arena.new_node(data);
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 1)
```
There is a shortcut to the above operation:

```
use atree::Arena;
let data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, token) = Arena::with_data(data);
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 1)
```
To add more data to the tree, call the [ append](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html#method.append) method on the tokens (we
can’t do this directly to the nodes because of the limitations of borrow
checking).

```
use atree::Arena;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 2);
```
To access/modify existing nodes in the tree, we can use indexing or
[ get](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.get)/

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.get_mut)

`get_mut````
use atree::Arena;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
// add some more stuff to the tree
let branch1 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
let branch2 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let branch3 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Slavic");
let lang1 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "English");
let lang2 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "Swedish");
let lang3 = branch3.append(&mut arena, "Polish");
// Access data by indexing the arena by a token. This operation panics if the
// token is invalid.
assert_eq!(arena[branch3].data, "Slavic");
// Access data by calling "get" on the arena with a token.
assert_eq!(arena.get(lang1).unwrap().data, "English");
// We can also do so mutably (with "get" or through indexing). As you can
// see, calling the "get" functions is more verbose but you get to avoid
// surprise panic attacks (if you don't unwrap like I do here).
arena.get_mut(lang1).unwrap().data = "Icelandic";
assert_eq!(arena[lang1].data, "Icelandic");
// On the flip side, we can access the corresponding token if we already
// have the node
let branch3_node = &arena[branch3];
assert_eq!(branch3, branch3_node.token());
```
We can iterate over the elements by calling iterators on both the tokens
or the nodes. Check the documentation of [ Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html) or

[for a list of iterators. There is a version of each of the iterators that iterates over tokens instead of node references. See the docs for details.](https://docs.rs/struct.Node.html)

`Node<T>````
use atree::Arena;

// add some more stuff to the tree
let branch1 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
let branch2 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let branch3 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Slavic");
let lang1 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "English");
let lang2 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "Swedish");
let lang3 = branch3.append(&mut arena, "Polish");
// Getting an iterator from a token and iterate

assert_eq!(&["Romance", "Germanic", "Slavic"], &children[..]);
// Getting an iterator from a node reference (that is if you already have it
// around. To go out of your way to get the node reference before getting
// the iterator seems kind of dumb).

assert_eq!(&["Slavic", "Indo-European"], &ancestors[..]);
// We can also iterate mutably. Unfortunately we can only get mutable
// iterators from the tokens but not from the node references because of
// borrow checking.

    lang.data = "Not romantic enough";
}
assert_eq!(arena[lang1].data, "Not romantic enough");
assert_eq!(arena[lang2].data, "Not romantic enough");
```
To remove a single node from the arena, use the [ remove](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.remove) method. This will
detach all the children of the node from the tree (but not remove them from

Returns the number of nodes the tree can hold without reallocating.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(1usize);
let initial_capacity = arena.capacity();
// capacity grows as nodes are added beyond initial allocation
for i in 0..100 {
    root_token.append(&mut arena, i);
}
assert!(arena.capacity() >= initial_capacity);
```

    .map(|x| x.data).collect();

    .map(|x| x.data).collect();

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/atree/arena.rs.html#419-472)#### pub fn [copy_and_append_subtree](https://docs.rs#method.copy_and_append_subtree)(
    &mut self,
    self_token: [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html),
    other_tree: &[Arena](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html)<T>,
    other_token: [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html),
)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/atree/arena.rs.html#419-472)

#### pub fn [copy_and_append_subtree](https://docs.rs#method.copy_and_append_subtree)(
    &mut self,
    self_token: [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html),
    other_tree: &[Arena](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html)<T>,
    other_token: [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html),
)

Copies a sub-tree from one arena and append to the given node of another. It does so by walking the tree and copying node by node to the target arena. Potentially expensive operation.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-3)Panics:

Panics if the token does not correspond to a node in the arena.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
use atree::iter::TraversalOrder;
let root_data = "John";
let (mut arena1, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
let node1 = root_token.append(&mut arena1, "Juan");
let node2 = root_token.append(&mut arena1, "Giovanni");
let grandchild1 = node1.append(&mut arena1, "Ivan");
let grandchild2 = node1.append(&mut arena1, "Sean");
let grandchild3 = node2.append(&mut arena1, "Johann");
let grandchild4 = node2.append(&mut arena1, "Jan");
// new arena
let mut arena2 = arena1.clone();
// append "node1" from tree2 under "node2" in tree1
arena1.copy_and_append_subtree(node2, &arena2, node1);
let mut node2_children = node2.children(&arena1).map(|t| t.data);
assert_eq!(node2_children.next(), Some("Johann"));
assert_eq!(node2_children.next(), Some("Jan"));
assert_eq!(node2_children.next(), Some("Juan"));
assert!(node2_children.next().is_none());
let mut subtree = node2.subtree(&arena1, TraversalOrder::Pre);
assert_eq!(subtree.next().unwrap().data, "Giovanni");
assert_eq!(subtree.next().unwrap().data, "Johann");
assert_eq!(subtree.next().unwrap().data, "Jan");
let mut tree2 = node1.subtree(&arena2, TraversalOrder::Pre);
assert!(subtree.zip(tree2).all(|(a, b)| a.data == b.data));
```

# Token in atree - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/atree/latest/target-redirect/i686-pc-windows-msvc/atree/struct.Token.html

`pub struct Token { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A `Token` is a handle to a node in the arena.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Creates a new node with the given data and append to the given node.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics:

Panics if the token does not correspond to a node in the arena.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
use atree::iter::TraversalOrder;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
let next_node_token = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
next_node_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
let mut subtree = root_token.subtree(&arena, TraversalOrder::Pre);
assert_eq!(subtree.next().unwrap().data, "Indo-European");
assert_eq!(subtree.next().unwrap().data, "Germanic");
assert_eq!(subtree.next().unwrap().data, "Romance");
```

#### pub fn [insert_before](https://docs.rs#method.insert_before)<T>(self, arena: &mut [Arena](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html)<T>, data: T) -> [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)

Creates a new node with the given data and sets as the previous sibling of the current node.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-2)Panics:

Panics if the token does not correspond to a node in the arena.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
use atree::iter::TraversalOrder;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
let child2 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let child4 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Slavic");
child2.append(&mut arena, "English");
// insert in between children 2 and 4
let child3 = child4.insert_before(&mut arena, "Romance");
// insert before child 2
let child1 = child2.insert_before(&mut arena, "Celtic");
let subtree: Vec<_> = root_token.subtree(&arena, TraversalOrder::Pre)
    .map(|x| x.data)
    .collect();
assert_eq!(&["Indo-European", "Celtic", "Germanic", "English", "Romance", "Slavic"],
           &subtree[..]);
```
Set a node in the arena as the next sibling of the given node. Returns error if the “other node” is not a root node of a tree (as in it already has a parent and/or siblings).

**Note**: for performance reasons, this operation does not check whether
the “self” node is in fact a descendant of the other tree. A cyclic
graph may result.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-3)Panics:

Panics if the token does not correspond to a node in the arena.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
use atree::iter::TraversalOrder;
// root node that we will attach subtrees to
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
let germanic = root.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let scots = germanic.append(&mut arena, "German");
let english = germanic.append(&mut arena, "English");
let romance = arena.new_node("Romance");
let french = romance.append(&mut arena, "French");
let spanish = romance.append(&mut arena, "Spanish");
germanic.insert_node_after(&mut arena, romance);
let mut iter = root.subtree(&arena, TraversalOrder::Pre)
    .map(|x| x.data);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Indo-European"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Germanic"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("German"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("English"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Romance"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("French"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Spanish"));
assert!(iter.next().is_none())
```

Creates a new node with the given data and sets as the next sibling of the current node.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-5)Panics:

Panics if the token does not correspond to a node in the arena.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
use atree::iter::TraversalOrder;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
let child1 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
let child3 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
child1.append(&mut arena, "French");
// insert betwern children 1 and 4
let child2 = child1.insert_after(&mut arena, "Celtic");
// insert after child 3
child3.insert_after(&mut arena, "Slavic");
let subtree: Vec<_> = root_token.subtree(&arena, TraversalOrder::Pre)
    .map(|x| x.data)
    .collect();
assert_eq!(&["Indo-European", "Romance", "French", "Celtic", "Germanic", "Slavic"],
           &subtree[..]);
```
Attaches a different tree in the arena to a node. Returns error if the
“root node” of the other tree is not really a root node (as in it
already has a parent and/or siblings). To attach a tree from a different
arena, use [ copy_and_append_subtree](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.copy_and_append_subtree) instead.

**Note**: for performance reasons, this operation does not check whether
the “self” node is in fact a descendant of the other tree. A cyclic
graph may result.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-6)Panics:

Panics if the token does not correspond to a node in the arena.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
use atree::iter::TraversalOrder;
// root node that we will attach subtrees to
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
// the Germanic branch
let germanic = arena.new_node("Germanic");
let west = germanic.append(&mut arena, "West");
let scots = west.append(&mut arena, "Scots");
let english = west.append(&mut arena, "English");
// the Romance branch
let romance = arena.new_node("Romance");
let french = romance.append(&mut arena, "French");
let italian = romance.append(&mut arena, "Italian");
// attach subtrees
root.append_node(&mut arena, romance).unwrap();
root.append_node(&mut arena, germanic).unwrap();
let mut iter = root.subtree(&arena, TraversalOrder::Pre)
    .map(|x| x.data);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Indo-European"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Romance"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("French"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Italian"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Germanic"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("West"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Scots"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("English"));
assert!(iter.next().is_none())
```
Detaches the given node and its descendants into its own tree while
keeping it in the same arena. To detach and allocate the subtree into its
own arena, use [ split_at](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.split_at) instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-7)Panics:

Panics if the token does not correspond to a node in the arena.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
use atree::iter::TraversalOrder;
// root node that we will attach subtrees to
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
// the Germanic branch
let germanic = root.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let west = germanic.append(&mut arena, "West");
let scots = west.append(&mut arena, "Scots");
let english = west.append(&mut arena, "English");
// detach the west branch from the main tree
west.detach(&mut arena);
// the west branch is gone from the original tree
let mut iter = root.subtree(&arena, TraversalOrder::Pre)
    .map(|x| x.data);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Indo-European"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Germanic"));
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
// it exists on its own
let mut iter = west.subtree(&arena, TraversalOrder::Pre)
    .map(|x| x.data);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("West"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Scots"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("English"));
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
```
Replace the subtree of self with the subtree of other. Does not remove self or its descendants but simply makes it a standalone tree within the arena.

**Note**: for performance reasons, this operation does not check whether
the “other” node is in fact a descendant of the parent tree of self. A
cyclic graph may result.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-8)Panics:

Panics if the token does not correspond to a node in the arena.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
use atree::iter::TraversalOrder;
// root node that we will attach subtrees to
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
// the Germanic branch
let germanic = root.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let west = germanic.append(&mut arena, "West");
let scots = west.append(&mut arena, "Scots");
let english = west.append(&mut arena, "English");
// the slavic branch
let slavic = root.append(&mut arena, "Slavic");
let polish = slavic.append(&mut arena, "Polish");
let russian = slavic.append(&mut arena, "Russian");
// the Romance branch
let romance = arena.new_node("Romance");
let french = romance.append(&mut arena, "French");
let italian = romance.append(&mut arena, "Italian");
// replace_node germanic with romance
germanic.replace_node(&mut arena, romance).unwrap();
let mut iter = root.subtree(&arena, TraversalOrder::Pre)
    .map(|x| x.data);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Indo-European"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Romance"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("French"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Italian"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Slavic"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Polish"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Russian"));
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
// the germanic tree is still around
let mut iter = germanic.subtree(&arena, TraversalOrder::Pre)
    .map(|x| x.data);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Germanic"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("West"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Scots"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("English"));
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
```

```
use atree::Arena;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
let first_child_token = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let second_child_token = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");

assert_eq!(siblings.next().unwrap().data, "Slavic");
assert_eq!(siblings.next().unwrap().data, "Hellenic");
assert!(siblings.next().is_none());
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/atree/node.rs.html#221-224)#### pub fn [preceding_siblings](https://docs.rs#method.preceding_siblings)<'a>(

#### pub fn [preceding_siblings](https://docs.rs#method.preceding_siblings)<'a>(
    &self,
    arena: &'a [Arena](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html)<T>,

Returns an iterator of references of sibling nodes preceding the current node.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let third_child_token = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Slavic");
root_token.append(&mut arena, "Celtic");

assert_eq!(siblings.next().unwrap().data, "Germanic");
assert_eq!(siblings.next().unwrap().data, "Romance");
assert!(siblings.next().is_none());
```
Returns an iterator of child node references in the order of insertion.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
let first_child_token = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let second_child_token = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
let third_child_token = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Slavic");
let fourth_child_token = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Celtic");
let root = &arena[root_token];
let mut children = root.children(&arena);
assert_eq!(children.next().unwrap().data, "Germanic");
assert_eq!(children.next().unwrap().data, "Romance");
assert_eq!(children.next().unwrap().data, "Slavic");
assert_eq!(children.next().unwrap().data, "Celtic");
assert!(children.next().is_none());
```

#### pub fn [subtree_tokens](https://docs.rs#method.subtree_tokens)<'a>(
    &self,
    arena: &'a [Arena](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html)<T>,
    order: [TraversalOrder](https://docs.rs/iter/enum.TraversalOrder.html),
) -> [SubtreeTokens](https://docs.rs/iter/struct.SubtreeTokens.html)<'a, T> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

Returns an iterator of tokens of subtree nodes of the given node.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
use atree::iter::TraversalOrder;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
let first_child = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
let second_child = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let third_child = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Slavic");
let first_grandchild = second_child.append(&mut arena, "English");
let second_grandchild = second_child.append(&mut arena, "Icelandic");
let fourth_child = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Celtic");
let root = &arena[root_token];
let mut subtree = root.subtree_tokens(&arena, TraversalOrder::Pre);
assert_eq!(subtree.next(), Some(root_token));
assert_eq!(subtree.next(), Some(first_child));
assert_eq!(subtree.next(), Some(second_child));
assert_eq!(subtree.next(), Some(first_grandchild));
assert_eq!(subtree.next(), Some(second_grandchild));
assert_eq!(subtree.next(), Some(third_child));
assert_eq!(subtree.next(), Some(fourth_child));
assert!(subtree.next().is_none());
let second_child_node = &arena[second_child];
let mut subtree = second_child_node.subtree_tokens(&arena, TraversalOrder::Pre);
assert_eq!(subtree.next(), Some(second_child));
assert_eq!(subtree.next(), Some(first_grandchild));
assert_eq!(subtree.next(), Some(second_grandchild));
assert!(subtree.next().is_none());
```
Returns an iterator of references of subtree nodes of the given node.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-9)Examples:

assert_eq!(subtree.next().unwrap().data, "Romance");
assert_eq!(subtree.next().unwrap().data, "Germanic");
assert_eq!(subtree.next().unwrap().data, "Slavic");
assert_eq!(subtree.next().unwrap().data, "Polish");
assert_eq!(subtree.next().unwrap().data, "Slovakian");
assert_eq!(subtree.next().unwrap().data, "Celtic");

# atree - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/atree/0.5.4/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/atree/

## Expand description

An arena based tree structure, backed by a custom allocator (ultimately
built on `Vec`) that makes node removal a possibility. On top of the basic
node insertion and removal operations, there are also many kinds of
immutable and mutable iterators provided for various kinds of tree traversal
operations.

Most of the code in the crate is `unsafe` free, except for the mutable
iterators, where the `unsafe` code is lifted from the core Rust
implementation of `IterMut`.

[§](https://docs.rs#general-guide-to-the-api)General Guide to the API

The crate consists of three main `struct`s: [ Arena<T>](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html),

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)

`Token`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Node.html)

`Node<T>``Arena<T>` provides the arena in which all data is stored.
The data can then be accessed by indexing `Arena<T>` with `Token`. `Node<T>`
is a container that encapsulates the data on the tree.As a general rule of thumb, methods that affect the memory layout such as
splitting and merging arenas, or methods to create and destroy nodes regardless
of existing tree structures like creating a free node, are defined on
`Arena<T>`. Methods that alter pre-existing tree structures such as adding
nodes with respect to existing ones ([ append](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html#method.append) or

[for instance) or splitting and attaching existing trees are defined on](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html#method.insert_after)

`insert_after``Tokens`.When it comes to iterating, iterators can be created from methods on both
`Token` and `Node<T>`. There are two versions of iterators, iterators over
tokens or references to the nodes. Both can be created by methods on `Token`
and `Node<T>`. However, due to the rules of borrow checking, mutable
iterators over the node references are only defined on `Token`.

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

- `serde`: support for serde 1.x. Optional feature/dependency.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage-examples)Usage Examples

We can start by initializing an empty arena and add stuff to it at a later time:

```
use atree::Arena;
let mut arena = Arena::default();
assert!(arena.is_empty());
// create a tree in the arena
let data = "Indo-European";
let token = arena.new_node(data);
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 1)
```
There is a shortcut to the above operation:

```
use atree::Arena;
let data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, token) = Arena::with_data(data);
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 1)
```
To add more data to the tree, call the [ append](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html#method.append) method on the tokens (we
can’t do this directly to the nodes because of the limitations of borrow
checking).

```
use atree::Arena;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 2);
```
To access/modify existing nodes in the tree, we can use indexing or
[ get](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.get)/

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.get_mut)

`get_mut````
use atree::Arena;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
// add some more stuff to the tree
let branch1 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
let branch2 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let branch3 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Slavic");
let lang1 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "English");
let lang2 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "Swedish");
let lang3 = branch3.append(&mut arena, "Polish");
// Access data by indexing the arena by a token. This operation panics if the
// token is invalid.
assert_eq!(arena[branch3].data, "Slavic");
// Access data by calling "get" on the arena with a token.
assert_eq!(arena.get(lang1).unwrap().data, "English");
// We can also do so mutably (with "get" or through indexing). As you can
// see, calling the "get" functions is more verbose but you get to avoid
// surprise panic attacks (if you don't unwrap like I do here).
arena.get_mut(lang1).unwrap().data = "Icelandic";
assert_eq!(arena[lang1].data, "Icelandic");
// On the flip side, we can access the corresponding token if we already
// have the node
let branch3_node = &arena[branch3];
assert_eq!(branch3, branch3_node.token());
```
We can iterate over the elements by calling iterators on both the tokens
or the nodes. Check the documentation of [ Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html) or

[for a list of iterators. There is a version of each of the iterators that iterates over tokens instead of node references. See the docs for details.](https://docs.rs/struct.Node.html)

`Node<T>````
use atree::Arena;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
// add some more stuff to the tree
let branch1 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
let branch2 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let branch3 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Slavic");
let lang1 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "English");
let lang2 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "Swedish");
let lang3 = branch3.append(&mut arena, "Polish");
// Getting an iterator from a token and iterate
let children: Vec<_> = root_token.children(&arena).map(|x| x.data).collect();
assert_eq!(&["Romance", "Germanic", "Slavic"], &children[..]);
// Getting an iterator from a node reference (that is if you already have it
// around. To go out of your way to get the node reference before getting
// the iterator seems kind of dumb).
let polish = &arena[lang3];
let ancestors: Vec<_> = polish.ancestors(&arena).map(|x| x.data).collect();
assert_eq!(&["Slavic", "Indo-European"], &ancestors[..]);
// We can also iterate mutably. Unfortunately we can only get mutable
// iterators from the tokens but not from the node references because of
// borrow checking.
for lang in branch2.children_mut(&mut arena) {
    lang.data = "Not romantic enough";
}
assert_eq!(arena[lang1].data, "Not romantic enough");
assert_eq!(arena[lang2].data, "Not romantic enough");
```
To remove a single node from the arena, use the [ remove](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.remove) method. This will
detach all the children of the node from the tree (but not remove them from
memory).

```
use atree::Arena;
use atree::iter::TraversalOrder;
// root node that we will attach subtrees to
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
// the Germanic branch
let germanic = root.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let west = germanic.append(&mut arena, "West");
let scots = west.append(&mut arena, "Scots");
let english = west.append(&mut arena, "English");
// detach the west branch from the main tree
let west_children = arena.remove(west);
// the west branch is gone from the original tree
let mut iter = root.subtree(&arena, TraversalOrder::Pre)
    .map(|x| x.data);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Indo-European"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Germanic"));
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
// its children are still areound
let mut iter = west_children.iter().map(|&t| arena[t].data);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Scots"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("English"));
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
```
To uproot a tree from the arena, call the [ uproot](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.uproot) method on the arena.
Note that will also remove all descendants of the node. After removal, the
“freed” memory will be reused if and when new data is inserted.

```
use atree::Arena;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
// add some more stuff to the tree
let branch1 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
let branch2 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let branch3 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Slavic");
let lang1 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "English");
let lang2 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "Swedish");
let lang3 = branch3.append(&mut arena, "Polish");
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 7);
arena.uproot(branch2);  // boring languages anyway
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 4);
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [iter](https://docs.rs/iter/index.html)
- A module that contains different kinds of iterators.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Arena](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html)
- A struct that provides the arena allocator.
- [Node](https://docs.rs/struct.Node.html)
- A node holds data in the arena. `Node<T>`can be accessed by indexing`Arena<T>``Token``get``get_mut``Arena<T>`, or through tree iterators.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html)
- A `Token`is a handle to a node in the arena.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- The Error type

let mut iter = root.subtree(&arena, TraversalOrder::Pre)
    .map(|x| x.data);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Indo-European"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Germanic"));
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
// its children are still areound
let mut iter = west_children.iter().map(|&t| arena[t].data);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Scots"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("English"));
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
```
To uproot a tree from the arena, call the [ uproot](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.uproot) method on the arena.
Note that will also remove all descendants of the node. After removal, the
“freed” memory will be reused if and when new data is inserted.

```
use atree::Arena;
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
// add some more stuff to the tree
let branch1 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
let branch2 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let branch3 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Slavic");
let lang1 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "English");
let lang2 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "Swedish");
let lang3 = branch3.append(&mut arena, "Polish");
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 7);
arena.uproot(branch2);  // boring languages anyway
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 4);
```

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/atree/latest/target-redirect/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/src/atree/lib.rs.html

# atree/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)#![doc(html_root_url = "https://docs.rs/atree/0.5.2")]
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! An arena based tree structure, backed by a custom allocator (ultimately
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! built on `Vec`) that makes node removal a possibility. On top of the basic
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! node insertion and removal operations, there are also many kinds of
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! immutable and mutable iterators provided for various kinds of tree traversal
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! operations.
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! Most of the code in the crate is `unsafe` free, except for the mutable
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! iterators, where the `unsafe` code is lifted from the core Rust
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! implementation of `IterMut`.
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! # General Guide to the API
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! The crate consists of three main `struct`s: [`Arena<T>`], [`Token`] and
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! [`Node<T>`]. `Arena<T>` provides the arena in which all data is stored.
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! The data can then be accessed by indexing `Arena<T>` with `Token`. `Node<T>`
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! is a container that encapsulates the data on the tree.
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! As a general rule of thumb, methods that affect the memory layout such as
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! splitting and merging arenas, or methods to create and destroy nodes regardless
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! of existing tree structures like creating a free node, are defined on
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! `Arena<T>`. Methods that alter pre-existing tree structures such as adding
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! nodes with respect to existing ones ([`append`] or [`insert_after`] for
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! instance) or splitting and attaching existing trees are defined on `Tokens`.
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! When it comes to iterating, iterators can be created from methods on both
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! `Token` and `Node<T>`. There are two versions of iterators, iterators over
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! tokens or references to the nodes. Both can be created by methods on `Token`
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! and `Node<T>`. However, due to the rules of borrow checking, mutable
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! iterators over the node references are only defined on `Token`.
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! # Crate Feature Flags
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!   - `serde`: support for serde 1.x. Optional feature/dependency.
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! # Usage Examples
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! We can start by initializing an empty arena and add stuff to it at a later
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! time:
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! ```
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! use atree::Arena;
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! let mut arena = Arena::default();
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! assert!(arena.is_empty());
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! // create a tree in the arena
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! let data = "Indo-European";
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! let token = arena.new_node(data);
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 1)
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! ```
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! There is a shortcut to the above operation:
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! ```
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! use atree::Arena;
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! let data = "Indo-European";
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! let (mut arena, token) = Arena::with_data(data);
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 1)
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! ```
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! To add more data to the tree, call the [`append`] method on the tokens (we
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! can't do this directly to the nodes because of the limitations of borrow
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! checking).
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! ```
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! use atree::Arena;
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! let root_data = "Indo-European";
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 2);
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! ```
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! To access/modify existing nodes in the tree, we can use indexing or
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! [`get`]/[`get_mut`].
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! ```
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! use atree::Arena;
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! let root_data = "Indo-European";
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! // add some more stuff to the tree
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! let branch1 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! let branch2 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! let branch3 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Slavic");
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! let lang1 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "English");
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! let lang2 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "Swedish");
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! let lang3 = branch3.append(&mut arena, "Polish");
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! // Access data by indexing the arena by a token. This operation panics if the
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! // token is invalid.
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! assert_eq!(arena[branch3].data, "Slavic");
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! // Access data by calling "get" on the arena with a token.
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! assert_eq!(arena.get(lang1).unwrap().data, "English");
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! // We can also do so mutably (with "get" or through indexing). As you can
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! // see, calling the "get" functions is more verbose but you get to avoid
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! // surprise panic attacks (if you don't unwrap like I do here).
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! arena.get_mut(lang1).unwrap().data = "Icelandic";
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! assert_eq!(arena[lang1].data, "Icelandic");
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! // On the flip side, we can access the corresponding token if we already
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! // have the node
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! let branch3_node = &arena[branch3];
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! assert_eq!(branch3, branch3_node.token());
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! ```
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//!
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! We can iterate over the elements by calling iterators on both the tokens
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! or the nodes. Check the documentation of [`Token`] or [`Node<T>`] for a list
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! of iterators. There is a version of each of the iterators that iterates
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! over tokens instead of node references. See the docs for details.
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! ```
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! use atree::Arena;
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! let root_data = "Indo-European";
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//!
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! // add some more stuff to the tree
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! let branch1 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! let branch2 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! let branch3 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Slavic");
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! let lang1 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "English");
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! let lang2 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "Swedish");
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! let lang3 = branch3.append(&mut arena, "Polish");
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! // Getting an iterator from a token and iterate
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! let children: Vec<_> = root_token.children(&arena).map(|x| x.data).collect();
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! assert_eq!(&["Romance", "Germanic", "Slavic"], &children[..]);
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//!
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! // Getting an iterator from a node reference (that is if you already have it
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! // around. To go out of your way to get the node reference before getting
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! // the iterator seems kind of dumb).
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! let polish = &arena[lang3];
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! let ancestors: Vec<_> = polish.ancestors(&arena).map(|x| x.data).collect();
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! assert_eq!(&["Slavic", "Indo-European"], &ancestors[..]);
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! // We can also iterate mutably. Unfortunately we can only get mutable
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! // iterators from the tokens but not from the node references because of
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! // borrow checking.
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! for lang in branch2.children_mut(&mut arena) {
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!     lang.data = "Not romantic enough";
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! }
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! assert_eq!(arena[lang1].data, "Not romantic enough");
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! assert_eq!(arena[lang2].data, "Not romantic enough");
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! ```
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! To remove a single node from the arena, use the [`remove`] method. This will
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! detach all the children of the node from the tree (but not remove them from
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! memory).
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! ```
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! use atree::Arena;
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! use atree::iter::TraversalOrder;
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! // root node that we will attach subtrees to
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! let root_data = "Indo-European";
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! let (mut arena, root) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//!
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! // the Germanic branch
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! let germanic = root.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! let west = germanic.append(&mut arena, "West");
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! let scots = west.append(&mut arena, "Scots");
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! let english = west.append(&mut arena, "English");
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! // detach the west branch from the main tree
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! let west_children = arena.remove(west);
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//!
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! // the west branch is gone from the original tree
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! let mut iter = root.subtree(&arena, TraversalOrder::Pre)
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!     .map(|x| x.data);
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Indo-European"));
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Germanic"));
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! assert!(iter.next().is_none());
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//!
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! // its children are still areound
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! let mut iter = west_children.iter().map(|&t| arena[t].data);
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Scots"));
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("English"));
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! assert!(iter.next().is_none());
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! ```
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! To uproot a tree from the arena, call the [`uproot`] method on the arena.
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! Note that will also remove all descendants of the node. After removal, the
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! "freed" memory will be reused if and when new data is inserted.
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! ```
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! use atree::Arena;
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//!
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! let root_data = "Indo-European";
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//!
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! // add some more stuff to the tree
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! let branch1 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Romance");
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! let branch2 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! let branch3 = root_token.append(&mut arena, "Slavic");
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! let lang1 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "English");
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! let lang2 = branch2.append(&mut arena, "Swedish");
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! let lang3 = branch3.append(&mut arena, "Polish");
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//!
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 7);
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! arena.uproot(branch2);  // boring languages anyway
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//! assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 4);
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! ```

# Arena in atree - Rust

`pub struct Arena<T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A struct that provides the arena allocator.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

let mut arena = Arena::default();

#### pub fn [node_count](https://docs.rs#method.node_count)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

Counts the number of nodes currently in the arena.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
let root_data = 1usize;
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 1);
let next_node_token = root_token.append(&mut arena, 2usize);
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 2);
next_node_token.append(&mut arena, 3usize);
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 3);
```
Returns the number of nodes the tree can hold without reallocating.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(1usize);
let initial_capacity = arena.capacity();
// capacity grows as nodes are added beyond initial allocation
for i in 0..100 {
    root_token.append(&mut arena, i);
}
assert!(arena.capacity() >= initial_capacity);
```
Initializes arena and initializes a new tree with the given data at the root node.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
let root_data = 1usize;
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
assert_eq!(arena[root_token].data, 1);
```

assert!(arena.is_empty());

Gets a reference to a node in the arena.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples:

```

let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);

Gets a mutable reference to a node in the arena.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
let root_data = 1usize;
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
let next_node_token = root_token.append(&mut arena, 2usize);
// get the node we just inserted
let next_node = arena.get_mut(next_node_token).unwrap();
// mutate the data as you wish
next_node.data = 10;
```
Removes the given node from the arena and returns the tokens of its
children. Use [ uproot](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.uproot) instead if you no longer need the descendants
of the node such that the freed memory could be reused.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics:

Panics if the token does not correspond to a node in the arena.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
use atree::iter::TraversalOrder;
// root node that we will attach subtrees to
let root_data = "Indo-European";
let (mut arena, root) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
// the Germanic branch
let germanic = root.append(&mut arena, "Germanic");
let west = germanic.append(&mut arena, "West");
let scots = west.append(&mut arena, "Scots");
let english = west.append(&mut arena, "English");
// detach the west branch from the main tree
let west_children = arena.remove(west);
// the west branch is gone from the original tree
let mut iter = root.subtree(&arena, TraversalOrder::Pre)
    .map(|x| x.data);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Indo-European"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Germanic"));
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
// its children are still areound
let mut iter = west_children.iter().map(|&t| arena[t].data);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("Scots"));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some("English"));
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
```
Removes the given node along with all its descendants. If you only
wanted to remove the node while keeping its children, use [ remove](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.remove)
instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics:

Panics if the token does not correspond to a node in the arena.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-9)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
use atree::iter::TraversalOrder;
let root_data = 1usize;
let (mut arena, root_token) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
let next_node = root_token.append(&mut arena, 2usize);
let nnext_node1 = next_node.append(&mut arena, 3usize);
let nnext_node2 = next_node.append(&mut arena, 4usize);
arena.uproot(next_node);
let mut iter = root_token.subtree_tokens(&arena, TraversalOrder::Pre);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(root_token));
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
// only one node is left
assert_eq!(arena.node_count(), 1);
// the node left is the root node
assert_eq!(arena[root_token].data, root_data);
```
Moves subtree with the root at the given node into its own arena. To
detach a given subtree root node from a tree into its own while
remaining in the same arena, use [ detach](https://docs.rs/struct.Token.html#method.detach) instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-2)Panics:

Panics if the token does not correspond to a node in the arena.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-10)Examples:

```
use atree::Arena;
use atree::iter::TraversalOrder;
let root_data = "a0";
let (mut arena1, root1) = Arena::with_data(root_data);
let node1 = root1.append(&mut arena1, "a1");
let node2 = root1.append(&mut arena1, "b1");
let grandchild1 = node1.append(&mut arena1, "a2");
let grandchild2 = node2.append(&mut arena1, "b2");
// split tree
let (arena2, root2) = arena1.split_at(node2);
let arena1_elt: Vec<_> = root1.subtree(&arena1, TraversalOrder::Pre)
    .map(|x| x.data).collect();
let arena2_elt: Vec<_> = root2.subtree(&arena2, TraversalOrder::Pre)
    .map(|x| x.data).collect();
assert_eq!(&["a0", "a1", "a2"], &arena1_elt[..]);
assert_eq!(&["b1", "b2"], &arena2_elt[..]);
```
